context: Real-valued function sequence on D subset of R, pointwise ε-N convergence / pointwise-real-quantifier-order
editorial_note: ProofWiki explicitly distinguishes real-valued pointwise convergence with ∀x then ∀ε then ∃N from the equivalent topological-space function-product formulation for arbitrary topological T. The real scope requires finite real pointwise limits but does not require uniform N; the quantifier order allows N to depend on x. Its topological product criterion is valid for arbitrary topological spaces using the product topology, including non-Hausdorff targets where limits may not be unique. The two source contexts should NOT be listed as globally equivalent mathematical definitions without explicitly identifying the real metric topology as a specialization; topological version is more general. For empty D, pointwise convergence holds vacuously for every f and every sequence, including the unique empty map. The source allows N∈R rather than N∈N, which is equivalent for integer n; our paraphrase chooses a natural cutoff. Uniform convergence is stronger for real target and is not to be substituted. The product-topology meaning is a separate prerequisite candidate, not fabricated if unscreened. Sections: Definition real-valued ε-N quantifier order, Topological-space section product topology equivalence, Comment comparison with uniform convergence
text: Let D⊆ℝ and f_n,f:D→ℝ. The sequence f_n converges pointwise to f on D if for every x∈D and ε>0 there is N_x,ε∈ℕ such that for all n≥N_x,ε, |f_n(x)−f(x)|<ε.

text: For a set D, a topological space T, functions f_n,f:D→T, the sequence f_n converges pointwise to f if and only if it converges to f as a sequence of elements of the product space T^D with its product topology.

context: Uniform convergence of mappings from arbitrary set S into metric space / uniform-metric-quantifiers
editorial_note: The metric-target and real-target uniform-convergence formulations share the ε-before-x quantifier order; a single N_ε works for the entire domain for n≥N_ε. The real target is a specialization of metric-target convergence using |a−b|; they have separate specified contexts, not two unrelated concepts, and the domain need not have any topology for metric-target uniform convergence. Uniform convergence implies pointwise convergence, not conversely: for f_n(x)=x^n on [0,1], pointwise limit is 0 for x<1 and 1 at x=1, not uniform because values near 1 stay near 1; the limiting function is discontinuous while each f_n is continuous. Crucial editorial source caveat: ProofWiki Infinite Series section writes s_n(x)=Σ_{k=1}^n f_n(x), not f_k(x), which is mathematically erroneous in general; it produces n f_n(x) rather than Σ f_k(x). Preserve this bad line as a held source observation, do not promote its false formula as a correct formulation or source-to-term link. Valid uniform convergence for a series is uniform convergence of the correct partial sums, but that additional context is not promoted in this pass. A cutoff N∈ℝ vs N∈ℕ is equivalent for integer sequence indices. Sections: Metric Space, Real Sequences, Infinite Series source typo retained only as held record
text: Let S be a set, (M,d) a metric space and f_n,f:S→M. The sequence f_n converges uniformly to f on S if for every ε>0 there exists N_ε∈ℕ such that for all n≥N_ε and all x∈S, d(f_n(x),f(x))<ε.

context: Locally uniform convergence from arbitrary topological X to metric target M / neighborhood-uniform-every-point
editorial_note: ProofWiki explicitly states the general definition: for each point x of topological X there is some neighborhood U_x on which the entire sequence of maps to a metric M converges uniformly. The neighborhood may depend on x, and the uniform N_ε may depend on the chosen U_x as well as ε, but is NOT allowed to vary with individual points y∈U_x. Global uniform convergence implies locally uniform; converse fails on noncompact spaces generally (e.g. f_n(x)=x/n on R converges uniformly on each bounded neighborhood, not uniformly on all R). Local uniformity is stronger than mere pointwise convergence. Source also gives complex-open-disc specialization and locally uniform series via partial sums; those are contexts with additional complex-function or series prerequisites not promoted here. No local compactness, Hausdorff property, or completeness assumed by the general version, except that metric targets are Hausdorff. Empty X satisfies the condition vacuously. Sections: General Definition, Complex Functions open-disk specialization not promoted, Series partial-sum specialization not promoted
text: Let X be a topological space, (M,d) a metric space and f_n,f:X→M. The sequence f_n converges locally uniformly to f if each x∈X has a neighborhood U_x⊆X on which f_n|U_x converges uniformly to f|U_x.

context: Nonzero eigenvector of a K-linear endomorphism for an eigenvalue scalar / nonzero-operator-eigen-equation
editorial_note: The source explicitly states both a nonzero vector lying in the kernel of A−λI and equivalently Av=λv. These are the SAME eigenvector meaning for a linear endomorphism over a common field K because (A−λI)v=0 is equivalent to Av=λv. Crucial nonzero condition: the zero vector always satisfies Av=λv, but it is NOT an eigenvector, so an eigenvector is a nonzero element of the eigenspace. A is a linear OPERATOR V→V, not an arbitrary linear transformation V→W with incomparable input/output for λI. The page assumes λ is already an eigenvalue rather than defining that term; no eigenvalue-target link may be invented if its mathematical source meaning is unavailable. The full kernel ker(A−λI) is an eigenspace and contains 0; do not conflate eigenspace and set of eigenvectors. 'Eigenfunction' applies in specialized function-space contexts and is not blindly synonymous for every abstract vector eigenvector. No finite dimensionality requirement is implied. Sections: Definition nonzero kernel criterion, Equivalent eigen-equation, Eigenspace separate concept
text: Let K be a field, V a K-vector space, A:V→V a K-linear operator and λ∈K an eigenvalue of A. A vector v∈V is an eigenvector for λ when v≠0 and A(v)=λv.
